P.4.title: Ideally, a program should be statically type safe

P.5.title: Prefer compile-time checking to run-time checking

P.6.title: What cannot be checked at compile time should be checkable at run time

P.10.title: Prefer immutable data to mutable data

P.11.title: Encapsulate messy constructs, rather than spreading through the code

I.4.title: Make interfaces precisely and strongly typed

I.9.title: If an interface is a template, document its parameters using concepts

I.10.title: Use exceptions to signal a failure to perform a required task

I.11.title: Never transfer ownership by a raw pointer (`T*`) or reference (`T&`)

I.12.title: Declare a pointer that must not be null as `not_null`

I.13.title: Do not pass an array as a single pointer

I.22.title: Avoid complex initialization of global objects

I.23.title: Keep the number of function arguments low

I.24.title: Avoid adjacent parameters that can be invoked by the same arguments in either order with different meaning

I.25.title: Prefer empty abstract classes as interfaces to class hierarchies

I.26.title: If you want a cross-compiler ABI, use a C-style subset

I.27.title: For stable library ABI, consider the Pimpl idiom

F.1.title: "Package" meaningful operations as carefully named functions

F.2.title: A function should perform a single logical operation

F.4.title: If a function might have to be evaluated at compile time, declare it `constexpr`

F.5.title: If a function is very small and time-critical, declare it `inline`

F.6.title: If your function must not throw, declare it `noexcept`

F.7.title: For general use, take `T*` or `T&` arguments rather than smart pointers

F.10.title: If an operation can be reused, give it a name

F.11.title: Use an unnamed lambda if you need a simple function object in one place only

F.15.title: Prefer simple and conventional ways of passing information

F.16.title: For "in" parameters, pass cheaply-copied types by value and others by reference to `const`

F.17.title: For "in-out" parameters, pass by reference to non-`const`

F.18.title: For "will-move-from" parameters, pass by `X&&` and `std::move` the parameter

F.19.title: For "forward" parameters, pass by `TP&&` and only `std::forward` the parameter

F.20.title: For "out" output values, prefer return values to output parameters

F.21.title: To return multiple "out" values, prefer returning a struct

F.60.title: Prefer `T*` over `T&` when "no argument" is a valid option

F.22.title: Use `T*` or `owner` to designate a single object

F.23.title: Use a `not_null` to indicate that "null" is not a valid value

F.24.title: Use a `span` or a `span_p` to designate a half-open sequence

F.25.title: Use a `zstring` or a `not_null` to designate a C-style string

F.26.title: Use a `unique_ptr` to transfer ownership where a pointer is needed

F.42.title: Return a `T*` to indicate a position (only)

F.43.title: Never (directly or indirectly) return a pointer or a reference to a local object

F.44.title: Return a `T&` when copy is undesirable and "returning no object" isn't needed

F.50.title: Use a lambda when a function won't do (to capture local variables, or to write a local function)

F.51.title: Where there is a choice, prefer default arguments over overloading

F.52.title: Prefer capturing by reference in lambdas that will be used locally, including passed to algorithms

F.53.title: Avoid capturing by reference in lambdas that will be used non-locally, including returned, stored on the heap, or passed to another thread

F.54.title: When writing a lambda that captures `this` or any class data member, don't use `[=]` default capture

C.1.title: Organize related data into structures (`struct`s or `class`es)

C.2.title: Use `class` if the class has an invariant; use `struct` if the data members can vary independently

C.3.title: Represent the distinction between an interface and an implementation using a class

C.4.title: Make a function a member only if it needs direct access to the representation of a class

C.5.title: Place helper functions in the same namespace as the class they support

C.7.title: Don't define a class or enum and declare a variable of its type in the same statement

C.8.title: Use `class` rather than `struct` if any member is non-public

C.10.title: Prefer concrete types over class hierarchies

C.12.title: Don't make data members `const` or references in a copyable or movable type

C.20.title: If you can avoid defining default operations, do

C.21.title: If you define or `=delete` any copy, move, or destructor function, define or `=delete` them all

C.30.title: Define a destructor if a class needs an explicit action at object destruction

C.31.title: All resources acquired by a class must be released by the class's destructor

C.32.title: If a class has a raw pointer (`T*`) or reference (`T&`), consider whether it might be owning

C.33.title: If a class has an owning pointer member, define a destructor

C.35.title: A base class destructor should be either public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual

C.40.title: Define a constructor if a class has an invariant

C.41.title: A constructor should create a fully initialized object

C.42.title: If a constructor cannot construct a valid object, throw an exception

C.43.title: Ensure that a copyable class has a default constructor

C.44.title: Prefer default constructors to be simple and non-throwing

C.45.title: Don't define a default constructor that only initializes data members; use default member initializers instead

C.46.title: By default, declare single-argument constructors explicit

C.47.title: Define and initialize data members in the order of member declaration

C.48.title: Prefer default member initializers to member initializers in constructors for constant initializers

C.49.title: Prefer initialization to assignment in constructors

C.50.title: Use a factory function if you need "virtual behavior" during initialization

C.51.title: Use delegating constructors to represent common actions for all constructors of a class

C.52.title: Use inheriting constructors to import constructors into a derived class that does not need further explicit initialization

C.60.title: Make copy assignment non-`virtual`, take the parameter by `const&`, and return by non-`const&`

C.62.title: Make copy assignment safe for self-assignment

C.63.title: Make move assignment non-`virtual`, take the parameter by `&&`, and return by non-`const&`

C.64.title: A move operation should move and leave its source in a valid state

C.65.title: Make move assignment safe for self-assignment

C.67.title: A polymorphic class should suppress public copy/move

C.80.title: Use `=default` if you have to be explicit about using the default semantics

C.81.title: Use `=delete` when you want to disable default behavior (without wanting an alternative)

C.82.title: Don't call virtual functions in constructors and destructors

C.83.title: For value-like types, consider providing a `noexcept` swap function

C.86.title: Make `==` symmetric with respect to operand types and `noexcept`

C.90.title: Rely on constructors and assignment operators, not `memset` and `memcpy`

C.100.title: Follow the STL when defining a container

C.103.title: Give a container an initializer list constructor

C.104.title: Give a container a default constructor that sets it to empty

C.109.title: If a resource handle has pointer semantics, provide `*` and `->`

C.120.title: Use class hierarchies to represent concepts with inherent hierarchical structure (only)

C.121.title: If a base class is used as an interface, make it a pure abstract class

C.122.title: Use abstract classes as interfaces when complete separation of interface and implementation is needed

C.126.title: An abstract class typically doesn't need a user-written constructor

C.127.title: A class with a virtual function should have a virtual or protected destructor

C.128.title: Virtual functions should specify exactly one of `virtual`, `override`, or `final`

C.129.title: When designing a class hierarchy, distinguish between implementation inheritance and interface inheritance

C.130.title: For making deep copies of polymorphic classes prefer a virtual `clone` function instead of public copy construction/assignment

C.132.title: Don't make a function `virtual` without reason

C.134.title: Ensure all non-`const` data members have the same access level

C.135.title: Use multiple inheritance to represent multiple distinct interfaces

C.136.title: Use multiple inheritance to represent the union of implementation attributes

C.137.title: Use `virtual` bases to avoid overly general base classes

C.138.title: Create an overload set for a derived class and its bases with `using`

C.140.title: Do not provide different default arguments for a virtual function and an overrider

C.145.title: Access polymorphic objects through pointers and references

C.146.title: Use `dynamic_cast` where class hierarchy navigation is unavoidable

C.147.title: Use `dynamic_cast` to a reference type when failure to find the required class is considered an error

C.148.title: Use `dynamic_cast` to a pointer type when failure to find the required class is considered a valid alternative

C.149.title: Use `unique_ptr` or `shared_ptr` to avoid forgetting to `delete` objects created using `new`

C.150.title: Use `make_unique()` to construct objects owned by `unique_ptr`s

C.151.title: Use `make_shared()` to construct objects owned by `shared_ptr`s

C.152.title: Never assign a pointer to an array of derived class objects to a pointer to its base

C.160.title: Define operators primarily to mimic conventional usage

C.161.title: Use non-member functions for symmetric operators

C.162.title: Overload operations that are roughly equivalent

C.163.title: Overload only for operations that are roughly equivalent

C.166.title: Overload unary `&` only as part of a system of smart pointers and references

C.167.title: Use an operator for an operation with its conventional meaning

C.168.title: Define overloaded operators in the namespace of their operands

C.170.title: If you feel like overloading a lambda, use a generic lambda

C.182.title: Use anonymous `union`s to implement tagged unions

C.183.title: Don't use a `union` for type punning

R.1.title: Manage resources automatically using resource handles and RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)

R.2.title: In interfaces, use raw pointers to denote individual objects (only)

R.5.title: Prefer scoped objects, don't heap-allocate unnecessarily

R.12.title: Immediately give the result of an explicit resource allocation to a manager object

R.13.title: Perform at most one explicit resource allocation in a single expression statement

R.21.title: Prefer `unique_ptr` over `shared_ptr` unless you need to share ownership

R.30.title: Take smart pointers as parameters only to explicitly express lifetime semantics

R.31.title: If you have non-`std` smart pointers, follow the basic pattern from `std`

R.32.title: Take a `unique_ptr` parameter to express that a function assumes ownership of a `widget`

R.33.title: Take a `unique_ptr&` parameter to express that a function reseats the `widget`

R.34.title: Take a `shared_ptr` parameter to express shared ownership

R.35.title: Take a `shared_ptr&` parameter to express that a function might reseat the shared pointer

R.36.title: Take a `const shared_ptr&` parameter to express that it might retain a reference count to the object ???

R.37.title: Do not pass a pointer or reference obtained from an aliased smart pointer

ES.1.title: Prefer the standard library to other libraries and to "handcrafted code"

ES.2.title: Prefer suitable abstractions to direct use of language features

ES.3.title: Don't repeat yourself, avoid redundant code

ES.6.title: Declare names in for-statement initializers and conditions to limit scope

ES.7.title: Keep common and local names short, and keep uncommon and non-local names longer

ES.11.title: Use `auto` to avoid redundant repetition of type names

ES.12.title: Do not reuse names in nested scopes

ES.21.title: Don't introduce a variable (or constant) before you need to use it

ES.22.title: Don't declare a variable until you have a value to initialize it with

ES.25.title: Declare an object `const` or `constexpr` unless you want to modify its value later on

ES.26.title: Don't use a variable for two unrelated purposes

ES.27.title: Use `std::array` or `stack_array` for arrays on the stack

ES.28.title: Use lambdas for complex initialization, especially of `const` variables

ES.30.title: Don't use macros for program text manipulation

ES.31.title: Don't use macros for constants or "functions"

ES.33.title: If you must use macros, give them unique names

ES.41.title: If in doubt about operator precedence, parenthesize

ES.42.title: Keep use of pointers simple and straightforward

ES.43.title: Avoid expressions with undefined order of evaluation

ES.44.title: Don't depend on order of evaluation of function arguments

ES.49.title: If you must use a cast, use a named cast

ES.55.title: Avoid the need for range checking

ES.56.title: Write `std::move()` only when you need to explicitly move an object to another scope

ES.60.title: Avoid `new` and `delete` outside resource management functions

ES.61.title: Delete arrays using `delete[]` and non-arrays using `delete`

ES.62.title: Don't compare pointers into different arrays

ES.70.title: Prefer a `switch`-statement to an `if`-statement when there is a choice

ES.71.title: Prefer a range-`for`-statement to a `for`-statement when there is a choice

ES.72.title: Prefer a `for`-statement to a `while`-statement when there is an obvious loop variable

ES.73.title: Prefer a `while`-statement to a `for`-statement when there is no obvious loop variable

ES.74.title: Prefer to declare a loop variable in the initializer part of a `for`-statement

ES.77.title: Minimize the use of `break` and `continue` in loops

ES.78.title: Don't rely on implicit fallthrough in `switch` statements

ES.84.title: Don't try to declare a local variable with no name

ES.86.title: Avoid modifying loop control variables inside the body of raw for-loops

ES.87.title: Don't add redundant `==` or `!=` to conditions

ES.100.title: Don't mix signed and unsigned arithmetic

ES.101.title: Use unsigned types for bit manipulation

ES.106.title: Don't try to avoid negative values by using `unsigned`

CP.1.title: Assume that your code will run as part of a multi-threaded program

CP.3.title: Minimize explicit sharing of writable data

CP.4.title: Think in terms of tasks, rather than threads

CP.8.title: Don't try to use `volatile` for synchronization

CP.9.title: Whenever feasible use tools to validate your concurrent code

CP.22.title: Never call unknown code while holding a lock (e.g., a callback)

CP.23.title: Think of a joining `thread` as a scoped container

CP.24.title: Think of a `thread` as a global container

CP.31.title: Pass small amounts of data between threads by value, rather than by reference or pointer

CP.32.title: To share ownership between unrelated `thread`s use `shared_ptr`

CP.43.title: Minimize time spent in a critical section

CP.50.title: Define a `mutex` together with the data it guards. Use `synchronized_value` where possible

CP.51.title: Do not use capturing lambdas that are coroutines

CP.52.title: Do not hold locks or other synchronization primitives across suspension points

CP.53.title: Parameters to coroutines should not be passed by reference

CP.60.title: Use a `future` to return a value from a concurrent task

CP.100.title: Don't use lock-free programming unless you absolutely have to

CP.110.title: Do not write your own double-checked locking for initialization

CP.111.title: Use a conventional pattern if you really need double-checked locking

CP.200.title: Use `volatile` only to talk to non-C++ memory

E.1.title: Develop an error-handling strategy early in a design

E.2.title: Throw an exception to signal that a function can't perform its assigned task

E.3.title: Use exceptions for error handling only

E.4.title: Design your error-handling strategy around invariants

E.5.title: Let a constructor establish an invariant, and throw if it cannot

E.12.title: Use `noexcept` when exiting a function because of a `throw` is impossible or unacceptable

E.13.title: Never throw while being the direct owner of an object

E.14.title: Use purpose-designed user-defined types as exceptions (not built-in types)

E.15.title: Throw by value, catch exceptions from a hierarchy by reference

E.16.title: Destructors, deallocation, `swap`, and exception type copy/move construction must never fail

E.17.title: Don't try to catch every exception in every function

E.19.title: Use a `final_action` object to express cleanup if no suitable resource handle is available

E.25.title: If you can't throw exceptions, simulate RAII for resource management

E.26.title: If you can't throw exceptions, consider failing fast

E.27.title: If you can't throw exceptions, use error codes systematically

E.28.title: Avoid error handling based on global state (e.g. `errno`)

T.1.title: Use templates to raise the level of abstraction of code

T.2.title: Use templates to express algorithms that apply to many argument types

T.3.title: Use templates to express containers and ranges

T.4.title: Use templates to express syntax tree manipulation

T.5.title: Combine generic and OO techniques to amplify their strengths, not their costs

T.10.title: Specify concepts for all template arguments

T.12.title: Prefer concept names over `auto` for local variables

T.13.title: Prefer the shorthand notation for simple, single-type argument concepts

T.21.title: Require a complete set of operations for a concept

T.23.title: Differentiate a refined concept from its more general case by adding new use patterns.

T.24.title: Use tag classes or traits to differentiate concepts that differ only in semantics.

T.26.title: Prefer to define concepts in terms of use-patterns rather than simple syntax

T.40.title: Use function objects to pass operations to algorithms

T.41.title: Require only essential properties in a template's concepts

T.42.title: Use template aliases to simplify notation and hide implementation details

T.44.title: Use function templates to deduce class template argument types (where feasible)

T.46.title: Require template arguments to be at least semiregular

T.47.title: Avoid highly visible unconstrained templates with common names

T.48.title: If your compiler does not support concepts, fake them with `enable_if`

T.62.title: Place non-dependent class template members in a non-templated base class

T.64.title: Use specialization to provide alternative implementations of class templates

T.65.title: Use tag dispatch to provide alternative implementations of a function

T.67.title: Use specialization to provide alternative implementations for irregular types

T.68.title: Use `{}` rather than `()` within templates to avoid ambiguities

T.69.title: Inside a template, don't make an unqualified non-member function call unless you intend it to be a customization point

T.80.title: Do not naively templatize a class hierarchy

T.81.title: Do not mix hierarchies and arrays

T.82.title: Linearize a hierarchy when virtual functions are undesirable

T.83.title: Do not declare a member function template virtual

T.84.title: Use a non-template core implementation to provide an ABI-stable interface

T.100.title: Use variadic templates when you need a function that takes a variable number of arguments of a variety of types

T.101.title: ??? How to pass arguments to a variadic template ???

T.102.title: How to process arguments to a variadic template

T.103.title: Don't use variadic templates for homogeneous argument lists

T.120.title: Use template metaprogramming only when you really need to

T.121.title: Use template metaprogramming primarily to emulate concepts

T.122.title: Use templates (usually template aliases) to compute types at compile time

T.123.title: Use `constexpr` functions to compute values at compile time

T.124.title: Prefer to use standard-library TMP facilities

T.125.title: If you need to go beyond the standard-library TMP facilities, use an existing library

T.140.title: If an operation can be reused, give it a name

T.141.title: Use an unnamed lambda if you need a simple function object in one place only

T.150.title: Check that a class matches a concept using `static_assert`

CPL.2.title: If you must use C, use the common subset of C and C++, and compile the C code as C++

CPL.3.title: If you must use C for interfaces, use C++ in the calling code using such interfaces

SF.1.title: Use a `.cpp` suffix for code files and `.h` for interface files if your project doesn't already follow another convention

SF.2.title: A header file must not contain object definitions or non-inline function definitions

SF.3.title: Use header files for all declarations used in multiple source files

SF.4.title: Include header files before other declarations in a file

SF.5.title: A `.cpp` file must include the header file(s) that defines its interface

SF.6.title: Use `using namespace` directives for transition, for foundation libraries (such as `std`), or within a local scope (only)

SF.7.title: Don't write `using namespace` at global scope in a header file

SF.8.title: Use `#include` guards for all header files

SF.9.title: Avoid cyclic dependencies among source files

SF.12.title: Prefer the quoted form of `#include` for files relative to the including file and the angle bracket form everywhere else

SF.13.title: Use portable header identifiers in `#include` statements

SF.21.title: Don't use an unnamed (anonymous) namespace in a header

SF.22.title: Use an unnamed (anonymous) namespace for all internal/non-exported entities

SL.2.title: Prefer the standard library to other libraries

SL.3.title: Do not add non-standard entities to namespace `std`

SL.4.title: Use the standard library in a type-safe manner

A.1.title: Separate stable code from less stable code

A.2.title: Express potentially reusable parts as a library

A.4.title: There should be no cycles among libraries

NR.1.title: Don't insist that all declarations should be at the top of a function

NR.2.title: Don't insist on having only a single `return`-statement in a function

NR.4.title: Don't insist on placing each class definition in its own source file

NR.6.title: Don't place all cleanup actions at the end of a function and `goto exit`

NL.1.title: Don't say in comments what can be clearly stated in code

NL.5.title: Avoid encoding type information in names

NL.7.title: Make the length of a name roughly proportional to the length of its scope

NL.16.title: Use a conventional class member declaration order

NL.19.title: Avoid names that are easily misread

NL.20.title: Don't place two statements on the same line

NL.25.title: Don't use `void` as an argument type

NL.27.title: Use a `.cpp` suffix for code files and `.h` for interface files
